\section{Background \& Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Test-time compute scaling.}
Test-time compute scaling encompasses three families: (a) extended chain-of-thought reasoning \cite{muennighoff2025s1}, (b) repeated sampling with majority voting (self-consistency; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}) and its extensions to free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}, and (c) best-of-$N$ selection via compute-optimal allocation \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
Reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} and adaptive gating variants \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive, wang2025make, feng2025optimal, kim2026reasc} reduce inference cost; \citet{chen2025twofailures} diagnose failure modes.
All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different aggregation mechanisms because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; \citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose two-stage entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction.
LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
Our entity-level construction aggregates across samples from a single fine-tuned model, without requiring model diversity or prompt engineering.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, xie2024selfimproving} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey, liu2025uqcc}, calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}, and abstention \cite{wen2025abstention}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} and self-evaluation guided search \cite{xie2023selfevaluation} learn per-sample scoring.
CISC \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc} and Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derive per-sample confidence from hidden states rather than output statistics, but require architecture-specific access to intermediate representations; these hidden-state signals remain untested for structured prediction (\S Limitations).

\section{Why Single-Signal Selection Fails}\label{sec:selection_gap}

Four of five signals assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input by construction (\S\ref{sec:formulation}); they estimate quality across instances but cannot rank candidates within an instance.
LP selection effectiveness depends on LP-quality alignment rather than degeneracy alone.
Cross-instance $\rho$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}) is attenuated by varying instance difficulty; within-instance $\rho$ directly measures whether LP discriminates candidates for a fixed input, making it the relevant predictor of selection success.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Best-of-$N$ selection (macro F1) on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, 2-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$). LP is per-sample; others use consensus-proximity. $^\dagger$One score per input.}
\label{tab:selection}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Method & NER F1 & $p$ \\
\midrule
Oracle & $0.775 \pm 0.001$ & --- \\
Greedy ($T{=}0$) & $0.645 \pm 0.001$ & --- \\
\midrule
LP           & $\mathbf{0.647} \pm 0.005$ & .29 \\
SJ           & $0.646 \pm 0.002$ & .67 \\
FK           & $0.646 \pm 0.001$ & .79 \\
EM           & $0.637 \pm 0.001$ & n/a$^\dagger$ \\
VC           & $0.623 \pm 0.004$ & n/a$^\dagger$ \\
\midrule
Random       & $0.610 \pm 0.003$ & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_selection_gap}
\caption{Correlation-selection gap on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Bars: QE $\rho$; line: $\Delta$F1 vs.\ greedy (3-seed mean). Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal outperforms greedy ($p{>}0.05$). Dashed green: oracle ($+13.0$\,pp); dotted gray: random.}
\label{fig:selection_gap}
\end{figure}

Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal outperforms greedy on SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}; Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}); the oracle reveals 13.0\,pp headroom, but LP achieves $+0.2$\,pp ($p{=}0.29$), below MDE (${\approx}$1.5\,pp; $n{=}529$).
The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
Few-NERD provides the definitive contrast: LP achieves $+1.39$\,pp ($p{<}0.001$) at low degeneracy (13.0\% vs.\ 17.8--67.9\%), while structural signals still degrade (VC $-1.79$, SJ $-2.14$\,pp; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).

\paragraph{Three governing factors.}
(1)~Instance degeneracy (SciERC 17.8\%, CoNLL 61.7\%); (2)~oracle headroom (CoNLL ${\approx}4$\,pp vs.\ SciERC 13.0\,pp); (3)~LP-quality alignment (Few-NERD within-instance $\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$ vs.\ SciERC $\rho{\approx}0.26$).
Across 23 configurations, degeneracy does not predict LP gain ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$; Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy_scatter}), though it causally modulates LP within fixed settings ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
The factors do not combine into a predictive model ($R^2{<}0$) but each is supported by controlled ablations (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{Adaptive Methods}\label{sec:adaptive}

Since instance-level selection fails (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}), we present approaches that extract value from multi-sample generation beyond single-signal sample ranking.

\subsection{Cross-Model Self-Consistency}\label{sec:cross_model}

Diversity from stochastic sampling within a single model is limited by architecture-specific degeneracy (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
Mixing samples from architecturally distinct models---which produce complementary error patterns---can partially bypass this bottleneck.

Combining 4 samples each from Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B (both fine-tuned on SciERC), LP-weighted entity construction yields $+0.42$\,pp over pure LLaMA sampling ($p{<}0.001$, 95\% CI $[0.27, 0.58]$; $N{=}8$ total).
The mixed ensemble exploits cross-architecture diversity: entities agreed upon by both families carry higher precision than those from either alone.

\subsection{Trained Entity-Level Verifier}\label{sec:verifier}

We train a LightGBM classifier on entity-level features (agreement count, LP, and consistency signals) to predict entity correctness.
Cross-dataset transfer on 7B fine-tuned models is negative (SciERC${\to}$Few-NERD: $-0.96$\,pp; SciERC${\to}$CoNLL: $-1.01$, $-1.64$\,pp vs.\ greedy; Appendix~\ref{app:verifier_transfer}), demonstrating dataset-specific feature mappings.
Under 72B zero-shot, transfer is positive ($+1.41$, $+1.51$\,pp) but approximately matches majority vote, suggesting gains derive from threshold calibration rather than learned discrimination.
This motivates approaches that generate training signal from the target distribution itself (\S\ref{sec:scd}).

\subsection{Self-Consistency Distillation}\label{sec:scd}

The verifier's negative transfer motivates an alternative: rather than training a cross-dataset classifier, use each dataset's own multi-sample consensus as supervision.
\textbf{Self-consistency distillation} (SCD) fine-tunes the model on entity-level labels derived from majority vote across $N$ unlabeled samples, teaching the model to internalize the aggregation step.
This avoids the feature-mapping transfer problem by generating training signal from the target distribution itself.
SCD evaluation is ongoing; we include it as a motivated direction grounded in the diagnostic findings above.

\subsection{Trained Verifiers: High Discrimination, Low Transfer}\label{sec:verifier}

A LightGBM entity-level classifier (5 features: agreement count, LP, VC, SJ, FK) achieves AUC${=}0.923{\pm}0.002$ under out-of-fold evaluation, confirming that entity correctness is learnable from the available signals.

Cross-dataset transfer remains negative (B2-v2: $-0.76$\,pp; B2-v3: $-1.02$\,pp on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:verifier_transfer}), confirming dataset-specific feature mappings.
Even a trained discriminator with near-perfect entity classification cannot close the aggregation gap, indicating the bottleneck is structural rather than a matter of signal quality.
This motivates approaches that generate training signal from the target distribution itself (\S\ref{sec:scd}).
